claims.text: Retention or loss of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by competition between nanoscale precipitate formation and deformation twinning.
Alloy composition, processing conditions, and operating temperature influence the competition between precipitation and deformation twinning.
The target materials are near-equiatomic, multiprincipal-element high-entropy alloys with an FCC crystal structure.
The target alloys are processed by mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering.
The controlled intervention substitutes Ti, Zr, or Hf for a fixed but unspecified amount of the base alloy while holding the processing route and microstructure constant.
The alloys are to be tested from room temperature to 800 °C under uniaxial tensile loading at a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1.
Composition and processing conditions influence the formation of nanoscale precipitates, including L1₂-ordered precipitates.
Composition and processing conditions influence the activation of deformation twinning.
Competition between nanoscale precipitation and deformation twinning changes the alloy's capacity for plastic deformation and energy absorption.
Changes in plastic deformation and energy absorption caused by precipitation and twinning govern toughness retention or loss.
At room temperature, mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering will produce a 20% increase in Charpy-impact toughness relative to the baseline alloy.
The baseline is a fixed-composition FCC high-entropy alloy such as CoCrFeMnNi produced by conventional casting.
The hypothesis applies to FCC high-entropy alloys made by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering and tested at temperatures no higher than 800 °C.
A lack of correlation between precipitates or twinning and toughness, or evidence that grain boundaries or dislocations dominate toughness, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Toughness being unaffected by transition-metal substitution would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention says microstructure will be held constant, while the proposed mediator and falsification experiment require composition-dependent changes in precipitates, twinning, and microstructural evolution.

The intervention calls for a constant processing route, but the predicted comparison contrasts mechanical alloying plus spark plasma sintering against conventional casting. This changes both composition and processing and therefore does not isolate the stated composition intervention.
